notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from the rich material gathered. I have substantial content from Enduring Word (David Guzik – charismatic/evangelical), Ellicott (Anglican), Gill (Baptist), Matthew Henry (Puritan/evangelical), and Ligonier excerpts (Reformed).

---

# Genesis 9 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 – God’s Blessing and Mandate

**Traditional Reading:** God blessed Noah and his sons with the same mandate given to Adam at creation: be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth (Genesis 1:28). Noah is the "second father of mankind" and the blessing is "exactly parallel" to that given to Adam, with additions arising from the post-flood situation. Ellicott notes man "starts afresh upon his task of subjugating the earth." Gill says the blessing is temporal, not spiritual, and the command to multiply was "peculiarly needful" since only four people remained.

- *Enduring Word (Guzik):* The world Noah entered from the ark was significantly different; this was a new beginning. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Ellicott:* Parallel to Adam's original blessing, with additions from the history of the past. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- *Gill:* A renewal of the blessing on Adam; more than a bare permission, carrying a promise of fruitfulness. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html
- *Matthew Henry:* "The blessing of God is the cause of our doing well." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

**Reformed (Ligonier):** The Noahic covenant is the first "sub-covenant" under the covenant of grace. God pledges to preserve the stability of nature so that He may enter history to save His people. The command to replenish the earth and institute capital punishment are covenant obligations. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/noahic-covenant

---

## v. 2 – Fear and Dread upon Creatures

**Traditional Reading:** Man's dominion over animals is re-established, but now based on "terror" rather than love. JFB says this dread "prevails among all the stronger as well as weaker" animals and keeps them away from human habitation. Guzik (Enduring Word) adds that since man could now eat animals, God implanted this dread for the animals' protection. Gill notes before the fall animals obeyed from love; now they flee.

- *JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):* Man's dominion is "now founded not as at first in love and kindness, but in terror." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/9.htm
- *Enduring Word:* If man could now eat animals, God helped the animals by putting fear within them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Gill:* Before sin, creatures obeyed cheerfully from love; sinning, man lost his power, animals rebelled; now dominion is renewed but they fear. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html

---

## v. 3 – Permission to Eat Meat

**Traditional Reading:** This is the first explicit grant of animal food to mankind. Guzik notes Adam was not given this permission (as far as Genesis reveals). JFB says "man was for the first time…allowed the use of animal food." Gill, however, disputes this, arguing that meat-eating before the flood is implied by Abel's offerings, peace offerings, and Jesus' description of pre-flood people "eating and drinking"; he sees this as a renewal, not a new grant.

- *Enduring Word:* Perhaps the earth was less productive after the flood's ecological changes, so God gave man permission to eat meat. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *JFB:* "Man was for the first time, it would seem, allowed the use of animal food." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/9.htm
- *Gill (dissenting):* This was not a new grant but a renewal; man had the right to eat flesh before the flood. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html
- *Matthew Henry:* This grant "fully warrants the use of them, but not the abuse of them by gluttony, still less by cruelty." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

**Modern Scholarship:** The NET Bible notes (netbible.org) were not reached in searches, but the scholarly consensus often sees this as part of the Priestly source's theology, distinguishing post-flood dietary rules from pre-flood vegetarian ideals.

---

## v. 4 – Prohibition on Eating Blood

**Traditional Reading:** The blood represents the life principle of the animal. Ellicott says the life is "God's especial gift" and the blood as its symbol must "be treated with reverence" — the life itself goes back to God. Matthew Henry sees a dual purpose: (1) to point forward to sacrificial atonement by blood, and (2) to check cruelty, lest men accustomed to shedding blood become callous toward human life. Guzik catalogs the importance of blood through all Scripture (Passover, covenant-sealing, atonement, Christ's blood).

- *Ellicott:* "Of this hidden life the blood is the representative…the gift itself must go back to God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- *Enduring Word:* Blood represents the life principle (Leviticus 17:11); respect is not based on superstition. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Matthew Henry:* The main reason is the shedding of blood in sacrifices as a reminder of the great atonement; also intended to check cruelty. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm
- *Gill:* The Jewish writers interpret this as the seventh of the "Noahide laws" — forbidding eating flesh torn from a living animal. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html

---

## vv. 5–6 – The Sanctity of Human Life and Capital Punishment

**Traditional Reading:** God requires an accounting for every human life taken — from beast or man. v. 6 establishes capital punishment: "by man shall his blood be shed." The reason is the imago Dei — man is made in God's image, giving human life inherent, sacred value.

- *JFB:* This establishes "the institution of the civil magistrate (Romans 13:4), armed with public and official authority to repress violence and crime. Such a power had not previously existed in patriarchal society." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/9.htm
- *Ellicott:* "This penalty of life for life is not to be left to natural law, but man himself…is to execute the Divine command." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- *Enduring Word:* The Bible distinguishes between killing and murder; the death penalty is appropriate for murder because life is valuable. Guzik cites Martin Luther: "God establishes government and gives it the sword to hold wantonness in check." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Matthew Henry:* "Wilful murder ought always to be punished with death." Whoever unjustly kills a man "defaces the image of God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

**Reformed (Ligonier):** The command to institute capital punishment for first-degree murder "indicates the high value that God places on the lives of His image-bearers." It is part of the Noahic covenant's binding laws that remain "until the end of the age." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-promise-noah

---

## v. 7 – Repeated Mandate to Multiply

**Traditional Reading:** The command to be fruitful is repeated to emphasise urgency — the earth needed repopulating. Gill adds it is "instead of taking away the lives of men, the great concern should be to multiply them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html

---

## vv. 8–11 – The Noahic Covenant Announced

**Traditional Reading:** God establishes His covenant with Noah, his descendants, and "every living creature." This is an unconditional, gracious covenant — God promises never again to destroy all flesh by a flood. Guzik notes God did not think the flood was a mistake; rather He guarantees the pre-flood conditions (imprisoned angels, shortened lifespans) will never be precisely duplicated. However, God will one day destroy the earth by fire (2 Peter 3:1–7), not water. Gill emphasises this is not the covenant of grace in Christ but a covenant of preservation with all creation.

- *Enduring Word:* The covenant extends to animals and the earth itself. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "Covenant engagements preserve the world from flood." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Gill:* "Not the covenant of grace in Christ, but of the preservation of the creatures in common." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html
- *Ligonier (Reformed):* This is the first sub-covenant of the covenant of grace; it provides "an arena" for God's special grace to operate. Everyone benefits — an example of common grace. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/noahic-covenant
- *Matthew Henry:* "As the old world was ruined, to be a monument of justice, so this world remains to this day a monument of mercy." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

---

## vv. 12–17 – The Sign of the Rainbow

**Traditional Reading:** The rainbow is the visible sign (token) of the covenant. Ellicott notes the Hebrew word is simply "sign," not "miracle." The bow may have existed naturally before, but now it is appointed as a covenant sign. Matthew Henry memorably says: "A bow speaks terror, but this has neither string nor arrow; and a bow alone will do little hurt. It is a bow, but it is directed upward, not toward the earth; for the seals of the covenant were intended to comfort, not to terrify." Guzik notes that the rainbow appears surrounding God's throne in Ezekiel and Revelation — God placed this reminder of His promise close to Himself.

- *Enduring Word:* The rainbow may have appeared for the first time after the flood because the water vapour blanket was released. God sees the rainbow around His throne as well as on earth. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Ellicott:* The rainbow is a "sign," not necessarily supernatural. God says "I have set" — the bow already created by natural laws is now appointed as covenant sign. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- *Matthew Henry:* The thicker the cloud, the brighter the bow; "as threatening afflictions abound, encouraging consolations much more abound." The bow is directed upward, not toward the earth. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm
- *Gill:* The bow is "without arrows" and points upward to heaven, a "token of mercy and kindness, and not of wrath and anger." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-9.html

**Reformed (Ligonier):** "Bow" translates the term for battle bows. God is a warrior who "hung up His weapon after the flood." He points His tool of destruction away from us. The rainbow prefigures the sacraments as "signs and seals of the covenant." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/signs-covenant

---

## vv. 18–19 – The Sons of Noah

**Traditional Reading:** Shem, Ham, and Japheth emerge as the three sons through whom the entire post-flood world is populated. Ham is noted as the father of Canaan — a detail Ellicott says is included because the Canaanites would take the place of the Cainites as a race associated with sin and judgment. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm

---

## vv. 20–21 – Noah's Vineyard and Drunkenness

**Traditional Reading:** Noah plants a vineyard, drinks the wine, becomes drunk, and uncovers himself in his tent. This is the first mention of drunkenness in Scripture. Ellicott says Noah was "scarcely aware, perhaps, of the intoxicating qualities of the juice," and that "he uncovered himself" is literally "he uncovered himself" — "no accident, but a wilful breach of modesty." JFB calls it a "solitary stain" on Noah's character, possibly from "age or inadvertency." Guzik emphasises this as a sober warning about alcohol's dangers, contrasting drunkenness with being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18).

- *Enduring Word:* A stark warning; alcohol is a depressant that loosens self-control. Contrasts with Spirit-filling which stimulates to better performance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Ellicott:* Noah was "scarcely aware" of fermentation's effects; the uncovering was "no accident." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- *JFB:* "This solitary stain on the character of so eminently pious a man" — perhaps from age or inadvertency. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/9.htm
- *Matthew Henry:* Recorded with Scripture's characteristic fairness — proof that "the best of men cannot stand upright, unless they depend upon Divine grace." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

---

## vv. 22–23 – Ham's Sin; Shem and Japheth's Honour

**Traditional Reading:** Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers. Shem and Japheth walked backward and covered Noah without looking. The sin was not accidental seeing but the mocking, dishonouring telling. Guzik notes the Hebrew says Ham "told with delight" — he mocked his father and undermined his authority. Ellicott concurs: "The sin lay not in seeing, which might be unintentional, but in telling, especially if his purpose was to ridicule his father." Some commentators (Guzik, citing Leviticus 18:6–20) suggest that "uncovering nakedness" language may hint at something more than mere looking — possibly a sexual act — which would explain the severity of the curse.

- *Enduring Word:* Ham "told with delight" — mocking his father. Possibly more than looking; "uncovered himself" and "nakedness" language is associated with sexual conduct in Leviticus. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- *Ellicott:* The sin was "in telling, especially if his purpose was to ridicule his father." Shem and Japheth acted with "filial piety" and "reverent delicacy." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- *Matthew Henry:* Ham "appears to have been a bad man, and probably rejoiced to find his father in an unbecoming situation." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

---

## vv. 24–27 – Noah's Curse on Canaan and Blessings on Shem and Japheth

**Traditional Reading:** When Noah awoke, he knew "what his younger son had done to him." Then he cursed Canaan (not Ham directly) and blessed Shem and Japheth. Several explanations exist for why Canaan, not Ham, is cursed:

- **Ellicott:** "His son, the little one" (Hebrew) means youngest son. Since Ham was not the youngest (Japheth was), Ellicott argues Canaan (Ham's youngest son, Noah's grandson) was the actual perpetrator. Origen and Aben Ezra preserved traditions that Canaan was the first to see Noah's exposure or did something worse than mock. Thus the curse falls on the actual offender. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- **Guzik:** Perhaps Canaan was also involved in a way not mentioned. Or the strongest punishment against Ham was for Noah to prophetically reveal the destiny of his son. God was not punishing Canaan for Ham's sin (Ezekiel 18:2–3); rather this was prophetic revelation of what Ham's line would become. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/
- **Matthew Henry:** Perhaps Canaan "was more guilty than the rest." The curse was fulfilled in the conquest of the Canaanites under Joshua and in the degradation of Ham's African descendants — though Henry adds that this "in no way excuses the covetousness and barbarity" of those who enslaved Africans. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

**The Blessings:**

- **Shem:** "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem." Ellicott notes this takes the form of a hymn of praise to Jehovah — the greatest of the blessings. Shem's line would produce the Jews and ultimately Christ "as concerning the flesh." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- **Japheth:** "May God enlarge Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of Shem." Ellicott sees this fulfilled in the Japhetic (Indo-European) nations receiving the religious privileges of Shem through the gospel. "Carried by Jewish missionaries, like St. Paul, throughout the Roman world, they have become the property of the leading members of the Aryan race." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm
- **JFB (on Japheth):** "A prophecy being fulfilled at the present day, as in India British Government is established and the Anglo-Saxons being in the ascendancy from Europe to India, from India over the American continent. What a wonderful prophecy in a few verses!" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/9.htm

**Important corrective (Guzik):** Some have used the "curse of Canaan" to justify African slavery, but Black people did not descend from Canaan. Canaan was father of Near Eastern peoples conquered by Joshua. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/

---

## vv. 28–29 – Noah's Death

**Traditional Reading:** Noah lived 350 years after the flood, dying at 950 — the same age as the antediluvian patriarchs. But Ellicott observes that "human life was fast diminishing" — Shem lived 600 years, Peleg only 239, and after Terah very few exceeded 200. "Before Shem's death the age of man was rapidly shortening." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/9.htm

Matthew Henry: "Noah lived to see two worlds; but being an heir of the righteousness which is by faith, he now rests in hope, waiting to see a better than either." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/9.htm

Guzik: "Noah was a remarkable man who served God in his own generation. Yet his last years did not seem to match the glory of his first years." His godliness is remembered in the New Testament as a man of faith (Hebrews 11:7) and a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-9/

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Perspectives (Where Found)

| Topic | Reformed (Ligonier) | Baptist/Puritan (Gill, Henry) | Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik) |
|-------|---------------------|-------|-------|
| The Noahic Covenant | First "sub-covenant" of the covenant of grace; arena for special grace; common grace for all | A covenant of preservation, not the covenant of grace in Christ (Gill); a "monument of mercy" (Henry) | God's gracious promise to all creation; rainbow surrounds God's throne |
| Capital punishment | Binding law until end of age; reflects value of God's image-bearers | Instituted for civil magistrate; wilful murder must be punished with death | The role of human government (Romans 13) to restrain depravity |
| Rainbow sign | Prefigures sacraments as "signs and seals"; God hung up His battle-bow | A bow without string or arrow, pointed upward; comfort not terror | God sees it both on earth and around His throne |
| Ham's sin | (Not specifically covered in search results) | Ham rejoiced at father's shame (Henry); mocking and dishonouring (Gill) | Possibly sexual in nature given Leviticus language; "told with delight" |
